items.name: Levi's
clues: Clothes, above all one item that almost everybody in this room owns.
Its founder left a village in Franconia, in northern Bavaria, for New York at the age of 18, and later moved to San Francisco during the Gold Rush.
He sold cloth and supplies to shops across the American West.
In 1873 he and a tailor, Jacob Davis, patented work trousers made stronger with small metal rivets.
Its leather patch shows two horses trying, and failing, to pull a pair of trousers apart.
The founder’s first name, with an apostrophe and an s. Famous for its 501 jeans.

items.name: Hellmann's
clues: Something you put on chips, in sandwiches and in potato salad.
Its founder left Brandenburg, south-east of Berlin, for New York in 1903.
In 1905 he opened a delicatessen in Manhattan, and one sauce on the counter soon outsold everything else.
Sales took off when he moved it from big stone jars on the counter into clear glass jars that customers could take home.
Since 1914 its label has shown a single blue ribbon, and it still does.
The founder’s surname. It’s one of the best-known mayonnaises in the world.

items.name: BioNTech
clues: Medicines, especially new treatments for cancer.
One of its founders came to Cologne from Turkey at the age of four; his father worked at the Ford factory there.
A married couple, both doctors, founded it in Mainz in 2008 with an Austrian cancer researcher.
In 2020, with an American partner, it developed one of the first approved COVID-19 vaccines.
Its headquarters are on a street called An der Goldgrube: “at the gold mine”.
Its name is short for “biopharmaceutical new technologies”.

items.name: Google
clues: Search, maps, videos, phones and an awful lot of adverts.
One of its founders was born in Moscow and left the Soviet Union with his parents at the age of six.
Two PhD students met at Stanford, and in 1998 the company started in a rented garage in California.
Its home page was famously almost empty: a logo, one box and two buttons.
On special days its logo is redrawn as a little drawing called a doodle.
Its name is a misspelling of “googol”, the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.

items.name: Steinway & Sons
clues: Musical instruments, especially big, black and very expensive ones.
Its founder, a piano maker from Seesen, a small town at the edge of the Harz mountains, emigrated to New York with his family in 1850.
He and his sons started the company in a loft in Manhattan in 1853.
Its concert grands became the instrument most concert pianists choose.
It has a second factory in Hamburg, which it opened in 1880.
The family anglicised its surname, Steinweg, and added “& Sons”.

items.name: Marks & Spencer
clues: Clothes and food and, according to many British people, the best underwear in the country.
Its founder was a young Jewish man who left the Russian Empire, from what is now Belarus, for England in the early 1880s.
In 1884 he opened a market stall in Leeds.
His stall had a sign saying: “Don’t ask the price, it’s a penny.”
Ten years later he went into partnership with a cashier, and the business grew into a chain of “penny bazaars”.
Two surnames joined by “&”. In Britain everyone calls it M&S.
